lesson.title: Gene Therapy: Treating Disease at the Level of DNA
lesson.summary: Gene therapy tries to treat disease by adding, correcting, or silencing genes directly, an approach with genuine medical successes but also serious historical setbacks that show it is still a developing technology.
lesson.body:
Many inherited diseases can be traced to a problem with a single gene, a missing gene product, or a gene whose protein no longer works correctly because of a mutation. A missense mutation, for example, changes a single amino acid in a protein, which can be enough to make that protein fold incorrectly or lose its function. Rather than only managing the symptoms that result from a faulty gene, gene therapy tries to treat the disease at its source, the DNA or RNA itself. This can mean delivering a working copy of a gene to replace one that is missing or broken, or, increasingly, using CRISPR-Cas9 style editing to correct a mutation or disable a harmful gene directly inside the patient's own cells. Getting genetic material into the right cells of the body usually depends on a delivery vehicle, or vector, often a virus that has been stripped of its disease causing genes using recombinant DNA technology and repurposed as a harmless courier for therapeutic DNA.

Gene therapy has produced real, approved treatments. Therapies exist for an inherited form of blindness caused by mutations in the RPE65 gene, for spinal muscular atrophy, a severe inherited disease of motor neurons, and, using CRISPR-Cas9 directly, for sickle cell disease and a related blood disorder called beta thalassemia, where a patient's own blood stem cells are edited outside the body and then returned to reactivate a healthy form of hemoglobin. These successes are genuine, and they represent decades of steady scientific progress.

At the same time, the history of gene therapy includes sobering setbacks that make clear it is not a uniformly solved technology. In 1999, an eighteen year old patient named Jesse Gelsinger died during a gene therapy trial at the University of Pennsylvania after his immune system mounted a massive, fatal reaction to the viral vector used to deliver the treatment. In the early 2000s, a French trial successfully used a retroviral vector to correct X linked severe combined immunodeficiency, restoring immune function in children who had previously needed to live in near total isolation. But several of those children later developed leukemia, traced back to the vector inserting itself near a gene that controls cell growth, a problem called insertional mutagenesis. These events did not end gene therapy research, but they forced the field to redesign safer vectors, screen more carefully for where genetic material integrates into the genome, and monitor patients far more closely.

Because of these risks, and because delivering genetic material precisely to the right cells in a living body is still technically difficult, gene therapy is best understood as a promising but still maturing set of tools, evaluated one disease and one vector at a time, rather than a single finished cure. Approved gene therapies are also extremely expensive, often costing well over a million dollars per patient, which raises its own questions about who can access these treatments even once they work.
